# CHAPTER 392

## THE CAMPER

The wagon north of Glass Cut had suspension designed by someone who hated kidneys.

Kel disagreed.

"It has suspension."

"Technically."

"That's what suspension means."

"Then it has hostile suspension."

Dask, across from me, looked interested.

"Hostility is difficult to measure."

Sori said, "Don't."

"I wasn't going to."

"You were."

"I was considering variables."

"That's how you start."

Vessa sat beside driver and ignored us.

Maro had fallen asleep.

Actually asleep.

Head against rolled tarp.

Mouth slightly open.

River-light specialist defeated by wagon.

I respected him more.

North road climbed away from Cut through low pine and pale stone.

Different country again.

Alder Basin had been wet work and ropes.

Glass Cut had been stone pretending eyesight was optional.

Here road ran dry between scrub, small farms, and occasional black marker posts with white ceramic caps.

I asked what they were.

Kel said, "Old flood return marks."

Dask opened mouth.

Kel added, "That is what everyone calls them."

Dask closed mouth.

Growth.

The road itself carried Glasswake residue in little ways.

Some wagon ruts shone when shadow crossed them.

Not in sun.

Shadow.

A fence nail blinked blue once as we passed.

One puddle reflected the wagon five seconds after wagon had left it.

I turned around to watch.

Sori caught me.

"Passenger again?"

"Research."

"With your mouth open?"

I closed mouth.

"Advanced research."

We reached marker thirty-two before midday.

Washout had eaten outer half of road.

Signed detour went uphill through orchard track.

Sign was good.

Rare luxury.

Kel stopped anyway.

"Wagon width."

Vessa got down.

We all did because apparently field work meant leaving perfectly good seats whenever terrain became interesting.

Detour track was narrow but firm.

Apple trees on one side.

Drop into muddy drainage on other.

Not cliff.

Enough to ruin wheel.

Kel measured with his body first.

One pace between inner rut and safe outer shoulder.

Then used folding stick.

"We fit."

Vessa: "Margin?"

"Enough if nobody gets creative."

I looked at Dask.

He said, "Why me?"

"No reason."

We walked first bend while Kel drove wagon empty of passengers.

Fine.

Second bend tighter.

Still fine.

Third had fallen apple branch across inner side.

Kel stopped.

I looked.

Branch maybe four inches thick at base.

Could move it.

Probably.

Then farmer appeared from orchard carrying saw.

"Leave it."

There.

Local person.

He cut branch.

We waited six minutes.

No Greg.

Retirement fund thriving.

Farmer said washout happened two nights before Glasswake, not because of it.

Important because people liked blaming magic for weather too.

Sori wrote route note.

Kel gave farmer half dried pear from lunch bag.

Farmer accepted like this was normal road tax.

Maybe it was.

Past orchard, road widened.

We rode.

By second bell I was bored enough to count ceramic caps.

Twenty-seven.

Then lost count because Dask asked why.

"Because I was bored."

"You could have asked me."

"For what?"

"Something to count."

"That's worse."

He looked genuinely offended.

Maro woke.

"Where are we?"

Kel said, "North."

Maro stared at him.

"I hate you."

"Good nap?"

"Yes."

Travel.

I liked it.

Nothing happened for almost an hour.

That felt new enough to matter.

Then we saw first lock tower.

Far away.

Black against afternoon sky.

Not West Locks proper yet.

Outer relay tower.

Tall narrow structure with three horizontal arms like someone built windmill and forgot wheel.

White cloth strips hung from upper arm.

None moved.

Wind definitely existed.

I looked at Maro.

He was already looking.

"Normal?"

"Sometimes."

Dask said, "Define sometimes."

Maro closed eyes.

Sori patted his knee.

"Don't kill him before camp."

We passed tower without stopping.

Vessa said it belonged Locks maintenance, not our current station.

Good.

Not every weird thing belonged to us.

Road camp sat another two miles north.

Calling it camp was generous.

Three roofed platforms.

One stone fire ring.

A hand pump.

Two privy sheds.

A low lockbox hut with survey seal.

And enough flat ground for wagon, which immediately made Kel happier than architecture deserved.

West Locks themselves were not visible.

But I could hear them.

Deep mechanical knocks every few minutes.

Not regular.

Water moving somewhere beyond hills.

Camp keeper was a woman named **Pella Dorn** with shaved sides of head, long braid, and one thumb missing at first joint.

She checked Vessa's papers.

"Six."

"Six," Vessa confirmed.

Pella looked at me.

"You the record hand?"

"Unfortunately."

"Then you get dry platform."

Dask said, "Why does he get dry platform?"

"Because last one ruined three days of paper sleeping under drip."

Dask considered.

"Reasonable."

Sori said, "I also have paper."

"You look mean enough to keep rain away."

Sori smiled.

"I like her."

Camp rules.

Water pump tested before use.

No washing dishes in drainage trough.

Food hung in iron box after dark because glass-mice came up from lock channels.

There.

"Glass mice?"

Pella looked at me.

"Mice. Eat glass salts. Teeth shine. Steal soap."

"Magical?"

"They're mice."

"That didn't answer."

"It answered enough."

Excellent.

No open flame after second night bell if east wind because lock vapor sometimes carried.

"Why?"

"Usually."

Kel wagon and mule.

"Promotion."

Cruel.

"Yes."

Could have optimized.

Didn't.

He did, muttering.

Crew life.

There.

Not coworkers in office anymore.

People who knew who snored soon.

This surprised me.

Not badly either.

Pot of beans, smoked meat, onion, some bitter green Pella had hanging by hut.

Maro chopped.

Sori claimed supervisory authority and was ignored.

Finally.

Kel first.

Sori and Dask off because Sori had dawn custody prep and Dask had first-light gauge calibration.

I looked toward Dask.

"Really?"

Kel walked away.

Asshole.

I got up.

Harness.

Crutches.

Blanket around shoulders.

Camp at night felt smaller.

Fire down to coals.

Wagon dark shape.

Mule asleep standing.

Survey cases locked in hut except overnight gauge box under platform.

Deep lock knocks came through ground more than air.

Thunk.

Long pause.

Thunk-thunk.

Water answered somewhere far off.

I sat near fire ring.

Watch did not require standing dramatically.

Good.

I listened.

First life watches had been different.

Sometimes six people asleep behind me because if I failed they died.

Sometimes enemy adventurers.

Sometimes nothing for eight hours except cold and thoughts.

I liked last one now.

At nineteen, again, I had learned boredom could be luxury.

Something moved near food box.

Tiny.

Scratch.

I looked.

Two points of pale blue light.

Then four.

Then six.

Glass mice.

Excellent.

Three little gray bodies emerged from drainage grass.

Normal mice except incisors glowed faint blue-white when mouths opened.

One climbed iron food-box leg.

Reached grease collar.

Slid down.

Tried again.

Persistent.

I whispered, "Respect."

Another mouse went toward soap bag hanging from peg.

Pella had warned.

I tapped crutch shaft lightly against stone.

Mouse froze.

Ran.

Others followed.

No spell.

No battle.

Bronze adventurer defeats mice with noise.

S-class legacy secure.

Five minutes later they returned from other side.

Smarter than expected.

I moved soap bag higher.

Victory through logistics.

Then east dark made sound.

Not mouse.

Soft footfall.

Pause.

Soft footfall.

I looked toward wagon.

Mule's ears were forward.

There.

Animal noticed too.

I stood.

Not locked in.

Attention sharpened one notch.

Tan shape at edge of moonlight.

Long legs.

Narrow chest.

Dog-like head.

Reed hound.

One.

Maybe.

No weapon in hand.

Knife at belt.

Quietly.

No need to spend more.

Took one step.

Good dog.

Maybe.

Another shape moved behind first.

Smaller.

Then third.

Three.

Not attack posture.

Interested.

Probably food.

Pella's partly sausage problem.

Threw it to land in dirt between us.

Not at animal.

One barked once.

Weird bark.

Almost cough.

"What?"

He sat up slowly.

Looked.

"Hadn't planned."

"Those are young."

One hound edged sideways.

Maro stood.

No hurry.

He took empty pot lid.

Hit it once with spoon.

CLANG.

All three vanished.

I stared at him.

"Advanced river-light technique?"

"Yes."

"Teach me."

"S-class prerequisite."

Fuck him.

He sat beside me.

"Your watch is next."

"I know."

"Then sleep."

"I'm awake."

"Your problem."

We sat.

Quiet.

There.

Not technical.

"Yes."

"Want to go back?"

I thought.

"Not yet."

He nodded.

"Good answer."

"Yours?"

"This is home-ish."

"Six miles west."

"Near."

"Dask was right."

"Don't say that."

Longer speech from him.

Rare.

"Then I left. Came back. Left again. Places don't care about your categories. You can belong somewhere and still be gone. You can hate a place and know every drain. You can love people and not want their street today."

I looked at him.

"That sounded rehearsed."

"It was not."

"Worse."

"I regret talking."

"Good."

He smiled.

Then pointed east.

One hound had returned.

Farther away.

Watching.

Maro lifted pot lid.

It left before clang.

Learning.

"Smart," I said.

"Enough."

There.

Enough.

I understood word differently now.

Not mediocre.

Not settling.

Enough could be exact amount required.

Enough strength.

Enough money.

Enough attention.

Enough Greg.

Reserve stayed reserve until enough stopped being enough.

Maro took watch early because awake.

I went back to bed.

Slept badly for first half hour because Dask did, in fact, grind teeth.

They did not glow.

Kel lied.

Morning arrived gray.

Pella had coffee substitute already boiling.

Tasted like burnt root and punishment.

Vessa had route sheet open.

"West Three slow. Four closed. Five cargo only. We take east gallery on foot, cases through Five freight cradle, regroup north landing."

There.

More infrastructure.

"Marsh shelf road. Mile Reed. North station by evening if pace holds."

"Hounds?"

Maro said, "Greg made friends."

"I did not."

Pella: "You feed them?"

"No."

"Then not friends."

Good.

Sori said, "Your teeth are loud."

He stopped.

"What?"

"You grind."

"No."

Five people looked at him.

Dask became offended by consensus.

"That is not measurement."

Camp packed.

Bedrolls rolled.

Food box checked.

Soap survived.

Glass mice had eaten tiny corner of one label on empty salt packet.

One night.

One dinner.

One watch.

One stupid mouse campaign.

Small.

Real.

Camper.

Again.

# CHAPTER 393

## THE RECORDER

West Locks sounded like giants arguing under floor.

Thunk.

Pause.

Grinding hum.

Thunk-thunk.

Then water.

A lot of water.

We left road camp before sun reached first lock tower.

Pella stood by wagon with coffee punishment in one hand.

"If east gallery shines, don't chase pretty."

"Wasn't planning to."

"Good. Keep it that way."

Kel climbed driver's bench.

Sori checked seals.

Dask checked Sori checking seals.

Maro yawned into sleeve.

Vessa said, "Move."

Camp disappeared behind first rise.

One night.

Already gone.

West Locks appeared properly ten minutes later.

Not one lock.

A system.

Three channels cut through low stone hills.

Gates taller than houses.

Black iron teeth fitted into pale masonry.

Walkways crossed at several heights.

Counterweight towers stood over channels with horizontal arms and white cloth strips like the relay tower we'd passed yesterday.

Some strips moved now.

Some did not.

Water sat at different levels on different sides of gates.

One basin almost still.

Another churned brown-white below half-open spill bars.

Freight cranes moved crates over channels without touching road.

Workers in dark wax coats shouted numbers nobody repeated back because apparently Locks people trusted screaming.

I liked it immediately.

Bad sign.

Vessa said, "Eyes on route."

"They are."

"Keep them there."

Approach office was small stone box wedged between West Three and Four.

Lock clerk wore red scarf and had ink on both wrists.

She read Sori's papers while talking to someone through wall tube.

"Survey six, east gallery foot, Five cradle cargo, north landing regroup. West Three slow but running. Four still dead. Five cargo window open until second bell unless priority grain comes early."

Sori: "False tones?"

"One before dawn. No gate movement."

Maro: "Floor shine?"

"East gallery lower panel again at first light. Maintenance marked and shaded. Walkable. Don't scrape it."

Dask: "Tone source localized?"

Clerk looked at him.

"No."

"Recorded intervals?"

"Yes."

"Can I see?"

"After your cargo window."

Dask physically suffered.

Vessa smiled a little.

"Move."

West Five freight cradle sat under square tower.

Not cage.

Cradle.

Long metal platform suspended by four chains, wide enough for two carts but currently loaded with grain sacks from opposite side.

No people allowed with reactive cases.

Same logic as Basin freight cage, bigger machine.

Our black case, gauge case, red repair case, food, and bedroll bundles went onto marked corners.

Sori checked each serial.

Cradle worker named **Hobb Fen** checked her check.

Dask watched both.

I watched Dask.

"You need hobby."

"I have gauges."

"That is work."

"Incorrect."

Hobb said, "If it makes him happy, don't ruin it."

Sori: "It does not make him happy."

Dask considered.

"It makes errors less likely."

There.

Best he had.

Cradle moved.

Chains tightened.

Counterweight dropped inside tower.

Platform slid out over West Five channel.

Below, water moved fast between open lower slots.

White strips on tower arm snapped once despite no gust.

Maro looked up.

So did I.

Nobody stopped cradle.

Not our decision.

East gallery entrance sat fifty yards downstream.

Foot route tunneled through gate wall itself.

There.

Different grammar.

Not catwalk.

Stone corridor wide enough for three people.

Rectangular openings every fifteen feet showed water at shoulder height on one side.

Then lower.

Then gone.

Because gallery moved through changing lock levels.

Floor slightly sloped.

Iron strips crossed stone at regular intervals.

Some warm.

Some cold.

I knew because crutch tips told me before hand did.

Not magic.

Temperature.

Probably.

At first lower panel, maintenance shade cloth covered section of wall and floor.

Yellow chalk boundary.

Worker stood beside it.

"Walk inner edge. Don't touch cloth."

We did.

Under cloth, pale light moved faintly.

Not bright.

Like moonlight under bedsheet.

Dask slowed.

Worker said, "Keep moving."

Dask kept moving.

Growth under threat.

I recorded as instructed:

EAST GALLERY LOWER PANEL
FIRST BELL + 18
SHADED BY LOCKS MAINTENANCE
PALE FLOOR/WALL RETURN VISIBLE THROUGH CLOTH
NO CONTACT

Maro looked over.

"Good."

Simple.

Useful.

We kept going.

First false tone happened while we were inside gate wall.

One deep bell note.

Not loud.

Felt through stone.

Everyone stopped.

Locks workers stopped too.

There.

Meaningful.

Second note did not come.

Worker nearest us looked at ceiling.

Waited.

Then shouted down gallery.

"No movement Four!"

Another voice answered farther away.

"No movement Three!"

Then wall tube whistled.

Worker picked up.

Listened.

"False tone. East tube, no gate travel. Continue foot."

Vessa looked at me.

"Record witness."

I did.

Tone time.

Location.

No observed mechanical movement from our gallery position.

Worker calls from Four/Three.

Authority message through wall tube.

No cause.

Dask said, "Duration approximately one and one-quarter seconds."

I looked at him.

"You have instrument?"

"No."

"Then observer estimate."

He looked offended.

Then nodded.

"Observer estimate."

Sori whispered, "He's learning."

"Terrifying."

East gallery rose toward West Four.

Four was open only enough to expose repair chamber above waterline.

Huge black gear tooth sat on wooden cradle beside wall.

Replacement tooth.

Almost as tall as me.

Actual gate gear had gap where old tooth had been removed.

Three workers fitted pins and measured seat.

No magic visible.

Maybe none.

Maybe everything.

Do not ask every noun.

At midpoint gallery narrowed around old support pier.

Not difficult.

Crutches through.

Right foot.

Body.

Done.

No identity crisis.

Then floor knocked under us.

Thunk-thunk.

Not bell.

Mechanical.

Water level in window opening dropped maybe six inches in seconds.

Maro watched.

"Three cycling."

Lock worker nodded.

"Slow cycle."

Dask asked, "How slow?"

Worker said, "Slow enough people complain."

Dask nearly died.

We reached West Five crossing just as our cradle arrived north side.

Hobb's counterpart checked cargo before release.

One bedroll bundle had shifted three inches inside marked box.

Sori recorded shift.

Nothing damaged.

Kel reset strap.

Normal.

Then one small brass custody tag slid off top of black case.

I saw it moving toward cradle grate.

Close.

Half pace maybe.

Could reach? No.

Crutches planted.

Sori was two steps away.

Hobb's counterpart reached too late.

I felt old instinct.

Tiny external push.

Not lock in.

Not big.

Same family as Dask's rolling marker.

This time deliberate.

Short.

Clean.

The brass tag changed angle.

Not stopped.

Just enough.

Hit raised case corner instead of grate.

Sori caught it.

Silence.

There.

Fuck.

Dask was not here.

Blessings existed.

Vessa was.

Of course.

She looked at me.

I looked at tag.

"Authorized?" I asked.

"No," she said.

"Safety?"

"Paperwork."

"Custody tag."

"Still paperwork."

Sori held tag.

"Expensive paperwork."

Vessa: "Did you touch equipment?"

"No. External effect only. Target was loose brass tag. No contact with case intended."

"Distance?"

"Half pace. Maybe less."

"One attempt?"

"Yes."

"Any pain?"

I checked.

"No."

"Any effect on anything else observed?"

"None observed."

She looked at Sori.

Sori: "I saw tag alter path. I didn't see case move."

Hobb's counterpart said, "I saw shiny thing not fall."

Useful witness.

Vessa sighed.

"Record separately. Not field-procedure approval."

"Understood."

There.

Second practical result.

First deliberate one outside training.

I did not feel stronger.

I felt annoyed at myself.

Could have yelled.

Sori might have caught anyway.

But effect worked.

That mattered.

Retirement fund analogy was dangerous if every successful trick became withdrawal.

This wasn't.

More like finding forgotten coin in coat.

Still mine.

Still real.

Protocol total, though.

One deliberate external attempt.

129 became 130.

I wrote it before memory could improve itself.

EXTERNAL ATTEMPT 130
FIELD / WEST FIVE NORTH CRADLE
~0.5 PACE OR LESS
LOOSE BRASS CUSTODY TAG MOVING
DELIBERATE
PATH CHANGE OBSERVED
NO CASE MOVEMENT OBSERVED
NO PAIN
NOT AUTHORIZED PROCEDURE

Hessa would hate handwriting.

Good.

West Locks north landing opened onto broad stone apron.

Behind us gate towers knocked and rang.

Ahead, landscape flattened.

Marsh.

Real marsh.

Low water glinted between brown-green grass.

Raised road ran on packed reed mats and gravel, slightly crowned above wet ground.

Tall poles marked edges every hundred yards.

Some had little hanging shells.

Wind made shells click.

Mile Reed was apparently not town.

Pella had used it like place.

It was marker district.

One enormous dead reed bundle wrapped around a stone post, taller than person, with painted number plate beneath.

Maro said, "Old distance marker."

Dask: "Not a mile."

Maro: "Nobody asked."

Sori: "I was going to."

Maro looked betrayed.

Road crew clerk at north landing stamped our exit.

Vessa asked route status.

"Marsh shelf wet but open. Two soft sections before Mile Reed. North station reports no closure. Reed hounds seen dawn, six or seven, kept distance from freight."

Six or seven.

Young three from camp maybe part.

Or cousins.

Not problem yet.

Kel collected wagon waiting north side.

Different wagon from camp route.

Lower wheels.

Wide tires.

Marsh wagon.

He approved.

"This one has suspension."

I climbed in.

"Hostile?"

"Normal."

We would see.

Road onto marsh felt softer even through wagon.

Ground moved subtly under wheel weight.

Not sinking.

Flexing.

Reed mats under gravel distributed load.

Nice.

Regional engineering.

Some sections had paired white stakes where road crew had added fresh bundles.

Water on both sides showed little bubbles.

Birds with long red legs picked insects from shallows.

One lifted and revealed four wings.

I stared.

Maro said nothing.

I refused asking face.

He waited.

I waited.

Dask broke first.

"They are splitwings."

I smiled.

"Thank you."

Maro looked disappointed.

We passed first soft section by walking beside empty wagon while Kel took it through one at a time.

Road worker had laid new reed bundles that morning.

No drama.

Second soft section had wagon ahead stuck to hub.

Merchant cursed mud.

Two road workers already unloading sacks.

Vessa asked if passage open.

Worker said, "Ten minutes if they stop arguing with gravity."

Merchant said, "I heard that."

"Good."

We waited.

Normal Greg.

Enough.

I sat on road edge with right leg stretched and checked hands.

No blister break.

Small hot spot at left palm.

Rewrapped grip cloth one turn tighter.

Sori sat beside me.

"Magic."

There.

"Apparently."

"You meant to?"

"Yes."

"Different from disk?"

"Disk was instinct before I thought. This one I chose."

"Useful."

"Maybe."

"You hate saying useful about yourself?"

"No. I hate turning two things into law."

She looked at me.

"Dask infection."

"Hessa infection."

"Worse?"

"Much."

She nodded.

"Vessa wasn't angry."

"She was Vessa."

"That is sometimes angry."

Fair.

Sori picked grass stem.

"You could train that while we travel?"

Question.

Simple.

Could.

Probably should, eventually.

Retirement account.

Withdraw little?

No.

Training wasn't emergency withdrawal.

That analogy had limits.

Maintenance mattered.

Compounding mattered too.

I smiled.

"Maybe. Controlled. Not while working."

"Dask will hear that from three miles away."

"Don't tell him."

She smiled.

"I already want to."

Merchant wagon moved.

We continued.

By late afternoon marsh widened until no trees showed west.

West Locks towers disappeared behind haze.

Road became narrow line through water and reed.

One reed hound appeared on far bank.

Adult.

Longer legs than camp juveniles.

Tan coat dark at shoulders.

It watched wagon.

Then trotted parallel fifty yards away.

Another appeared behind.

Then three.

Nobody reached for weapon.

Kel said, "Pella's friends."

"Not mine."

Maro: "You fed them emotionally."

"I said no."

"Strong bond."

They followed for almost mile.

Never closer than forty yards.

At one point one bounded through reeds and came out with rat in mouth.

Excellent.

Not interested in us.

Mostly.

Mile Reed marker stood at road fork.

Huge bundled reed post blackened with age.

Small shelter beside it.

No settlement.

A woman sold boiled eggs and smoked eel from basket.

Road traffic made market wherever road paused.

Vessa allowed ten minutes.

Survey food covered meal later, but this was not meal.

I bought nothing.

Not because poor.

Because smoked eel looked judgmental.

Orin would understand.

Dask bought egg.

Then measured shell thickness with thumbnail.

Seller told him to leave.

He ate egg outside basket range.

North station appeared before evening.

Stone base.

Wood upper room.

Signal mast with three black arms.

One stable.

One angled.

One moving slowly despite wind direction.

Here we go.

Station keeper came down steps before wagon stopped.

"Survey?"

Vessa handed papers.

Keeper skimmed.

"West Locks?"

"Crossed."

"Any false tones?"

"One in east gallery. No observed gate movement. Recorded."

Keeper nodded.

"Good. We got one through mast twenty minutes ago."

Maro looked up.

"Tone relay?"

"Maybe. Arm two moved with it. No wind match."

Dask was already opening notebook.

Of course.

Vessa looked at me.

Not lock in.

Just work.

"Greg, records with Dask."

"Yes."

There.

Recorder.

That was today.

Not hero.

Not S-class ghost.

Not passenger anymore.

I had crossed working magic older than some towns, watched gates lie with bells, deliberately moved a tiny piece of brass without touching it, and spent most of day writing down what other people actually knew.

Good job.

Useful job.

At north station table I opened notebook to clean page.

Dask sat opposite.

He glanced at my external-attempt note.

Stopped.

Looked up slowly.

"You did what?"

Fuck.

Sori, from doorway, laughed before I answered.

Recorder.

Apparently tomorrow might be worse.
# CHAPTER 394

## THE PRACTITIONER

Dask stared at my notebook like it had personally insulted him.

"You did what?"

"Moved tag."

"On purpose?"

"Yes."

"How far?"

"Half pace. Maybe less."

"Moving target?"

"Sliding."

"Single attempt?"

"Yes."

"And you didn't tell me?"

"I wrote it down."

He looked at notebook.

Then me.

"That is not telling me."

Sori, sorting custody sheets at other end of table, said, "It is literally telling everyone forever."

"Not same."

"Better, actually."

North station had one main room, one narrow records room, and apparently enough opinions for six people.

Outside, mast arm two moved again.

Slow.

Wrong direction for wind.

Nobody panicked.

Station keeper, **Rett Morn**, leaned out door and watched.

"There."

Dask abandoned me instantly.

Good.

He ran outside with gauge board.

Maro followed.

Vessa pointed at me.

"Records."

"I know."

"Good."

Normal work.

Excellent.

I took station log from Rett.

Arm two movement first observed twenty-three minutes before our arrival.

Single low tone through mast shortly before that.

No weather change recorded.

No freight bell scheduled.

No lock command due.

West Locks false tone earlier separated by more than an hour.

Do not connect because both tones.

I wrote exact times where known.

Approximate where not.

Rett watched my page.

"You always write uncertainty like accusation?"

"It deserves representation."

"Huh."

He had one of those faces built for weather.

Deep lines, red nose, gray beard cut short.

Probably fifty.

Maybe forty and north wind had opinions.

He tapped station log.

"Arm moved twice before you came. Once after. Never did that last year."

"How old mast?"

"Older than station roof. Younger than stone base."

"Useful."

"You asked."

Fair.

Outside, Dask called, "Greg!"

I went.

Mast stood thirty feet from station on square stone plinth.

Three black arms mounted on vertical shaft.

Arm one east-west.

Two angled northwest.

Three nearly vertical.

Wind came south.

White thread tied by Rett to arm two fluttered south-to-north.

Arm itself crept west.

Not with thread.

Maro had brass disk out.

Dask had two rulers, because of course.

"Record," Vessa said.

I did.

Arm moved maybe two finger-widths over forty breaths.

Then stopped.

No tone.

No visible shaft movement on arms one or three.

Maro said, "Could be residual return in mast body."

Dask: "Could be bearing creep."

Rett: "Could be haunted."

Sori came outside.

"Official category?"

"Very."

Rett smiled.

Vessa said, "No climbing. No disassembly. Station sends notice to regional relay desk. We compare record, then move on schedule."

There.

Bounded.

North station was not our new home.

Dinner was station stew.

I asked what was in it.

Rett said, "Food."

I stopped asking.

Dask did not.

He identified turnip, barley, smoked bird, and one herb Rett refused to name on principle.

Then Dask returned to me.

"Four attempts."

I ate.

"Hello to you too."

"We agreed."

"We tentatively agreed to controlled comparison after future work if conditions allow."

For today.

Fighter.

"How bad?"

"Normal bad."

Dask said, "That is not category."

Everyone ignored him.

Wind cut was narrow saddle between two stone shoulders.

Road crossed exposed for maybe sixty yards.

Black chain ran waist-high along uphill side between hooks.

Local sign:

HIGH WIND
ONE HAND / LINE OR RAIL
NO LOOSE LOAD
WAIT ON RED FLAG

Flag green.

Fine.

One hand line.

Problem.

I had two crutches.

Maro said, "There is lower route. Adds half mile."

I looked at saddle.

Could do it.

Probably.

Right shoulder still compromised.

One-hand line meant one crutch and one foot, ugly.

Harness maybe.

No.

Vessa asked, "What do you want?"

There.

Not can.

Want.

I wanted upper route.

I also wanted not to be idiot two days after shoulder strain.

"Lower."

Dask looked at me.

No comment.

Good man.

We took lower.

Longer path cut behind stone shoulder through little ravine.

Protected wind.

More distance.

Less stupid.

Patient becoming annoying identity.

Halfway through ravine, we found wagon.

Not ours.

Small two-wheel freight cart tipped against wall.

One wheel off.

Driver sitting on rock with bandaged hand.

Young woman standing over broken axle pin swearing continuously.

Not short Greg swearing.

Long narrative swearing.

"I told him, I told him if that pin went twice in wet season it was going to go again because wet season isn't fucking magic that resets iron, and he says no no, Mora, you grease it and it forgives you, like iron has religion, and now look, now fucking look at it."

There.

Dialogue variance alive.

Kel stopped.

"Need help?"

Mora said, "Need new pin. Unless one of you is secretly blacksmith."

Dask almost raised hand.

Sori physically put hand on his sleeve.

"No."

Driver said, "We have spare blank. Need fit."

Kel checked.

"I can shave wood, not iron."

Mora pointed north.

"Greyhook yard has fitter. Two miles. Cart blocks half path but people can pass. We'll sit."

No emergency.

No Greg.

Except something under cart caught my eye.

Small metal disk in dirt.

Not theirs maybe.

I pointed.

"Yours?"

Mora looked.

"No."

Driver leaned.

"Old hook token."

Maro said, "Don't pick yet."

There.

Interesting.

Disk iron-gray, maybe two inches across, square hole center, one edge polished bright.

Half buried near old anchor socket in ravine wall.

Mora said, "Those wash out sometimes. Freight tally thing."

Driver corrected, "Storm tally."

"Whatever."

Dask crouched.

"Not same."

Sori said, "Of course not."

Maro looked at socket.

"Could belong old anchor system."

"Useful?" I asked.

"Maybe historically."

"Magical?"

"Maybe not."

Dask: "Could be reactive iron."

Mora: "Could be trash."

Best answer.

I did not pick it.

Not because scared.

Because local road had owner system.

Vessa asked Mora, "Road authority claim salvage?"

There.

No free loot.

Vessa marked location for road notice.

We continued.

Greg wanted disk.

Greg had just bought quietener.

Greg could survive wanting two things.

Growth.

Greyhook Rise appeared near fourth bell.

Not town.

Fortified work ridge.

Stone terraces cut into hill.

Wind towers with big slatted arms.

Freight yard.

Repair sheds.

Rows of anchor chains hanging from frames.

One long public stair climbed center ridge like challenge written personally at me.

No.

Side ramp existed.

Good civilization.

At entrance, road board listed upper return beds and something new:

**NORTH REACH SURVEY HOLD - WEATHER WINDOW PENDING**

Vessa read.

"That's us."

Good.

Greyhook station lead came out before we entered.

Tall woman in red coat with hair braided tight against wind.

"River Survey?"

Vessa handed papers.

Woman scanned.

"You're late enough to be interesting but not late enough to be problem."

"Three Posts delay."

"Heard. Hounds."

Her eyes found me.

Of course.

"Crutch man?"

"Unfortunately."

"Don't fight anything here. Wind does enough."

"Strong policy."

She introduced herself **Aven Ro**.

Greyhook road/survey liaison.

Different speech.

Fast, declarative, no patience.

"North Reach weather window opens maybe tomorrow second bell, maybe not. Upper return beds walkable. Final ridge isn't. Crosswind. We hold crews here until tower strips agree for full half bell."

Vessa: "Any alternate?"

"Lower freight tunnel, closed collapse inspection. West shelf mule line, cargo only and miserable. So wait."

There.

Adventure.

Weather.

Not enemy.

Aven continued.

"You have two nights authorized if weather holds bad. After that route order recalculates. Bunks six. Food ugly. Baths nonexistent. Market tiny. Repair yard excellent."

Repair yard.

I looked at crutch.

Aven noticed.

"That thing bitten?"

"Yes."

"Bring to Rusk. He repairs staff shafts, poles, crutch wood if hardware standard."

There.

Useful.

Not artifact.

Actual road life.

We entered.

Greyhook wind made everything louder.

Chains knocked.

Tower slats clapped.

People shouted from twenty feet because otherwise conversation belonged sky.

I liked it.

Shoulder hurt.

Quietener in bag.

Fifteen copper left.

Road north temporarily held by weather.

And somewhere behind us, an old iron token waited in dirt for Road authority to decide whether it was trash.

Customer.

Not every thing.

That felt more dangerous than buying nothing.

Because now I had started.
# CHAPTER 398

## THE REPAIRMAN

Rusk looked at my crutch and said, "Dog?"

"Reed hound."

"Dog with wet opinions."

Fair.

Greyhook repair yard occupied half a terrace below freight anchors.

Three open-sided sheds.

Two saw benches.

Iron brazier.

Rows of staff shafts, wagon poles, chain hooks, replacement slats, and enough clamps to restrain a small god.

Wind moved through everything.

Not gusts.

Constant pressure.

Every loose strap had somewhere to slap.

Every hanging tool had been tied twice.

Rusk was maybe sixty.

Maybe forty-five with weather.

Hard to tell here.

Broad shoulders.

White beard cut short.

Two missing fingertips on left hand.

He took my right crutch only after I handed it over.

Good start.

Rolled shaft.

Pressed thumb around tooth grooves.

Held it near ear and flexed gently.

Then looked at me.

"You hit dog with this too?"

"Yes."

"After it bit?"

"Before and after."

"Mm."

That sound contained judgment and professional interest.

He set crutch on padded bench.

"Wood's sound. Deepest tooth got through finish, not through working depth. Hand grip fine. Upper cuff fine. Tip fine."

I relaxed more than expected.

Rusk noticed.

"You like these."

"I need these."

"Different."

"Both."

He nodded.

"Also different."

There.

Repair people.

He proposed shallow resin fill in grooves, wrap reinforcement around deepest mark, re-seal shaft.

Not structural splice.

Not replacement.

"Cost?"

"Assignment?"

Vessa from behind me said, "Personal equipment damaged during field incident under assignment. Reasonable repair covered if standard."

Rusk looked at her.

"Reasonable is ugly word."

"Use cheaper one."

"Covered."

Excellent.

No copper.

Economy liked paperwork sometimes.

"How long?" I asked.

"Hour if wind behaves. Two if it doesn't."

I looked outside.

Wind stole a rag off peg despite being tied.

Rusk watched it snap at cord.

"Two."

Fair.

He pointed at my shoulder.

"You favoring right?"

"Little."

"Then sit somewhere. Don't practice being heroic in my yard."

Everyone had same advice now.

I was becoming predictable.

I sat on low crate beside shed wall.

Left crutch across knees.

Right shoulder dull ache.

Better than yesterday.

Still there.

Greyhook weather hold had turned whole ridge into temporary city of people waiting professionally.

Freight crews played cards under chain awning.

Two mule handlers argued about salt blocks.

Wind tower operators walked terrace lines checking cloth strips, vanes, and weighted cords.

One woman spent ten minutes retying same canvas cover because wind wanted job too.

There.

New ecology.

Work shaped by air instead of water.

Dask arrived carrying my wrapped line quietener like sacred relic.

I frowned.

"Why do you have that?"

He stopped.

"Sori gave it to me."

Sori from doorway said, "I gave him the bag because you left it on bunk. I did not give him permission to unwrap anything."

Dask held package farther from body.

"It remains wrapped."

"Good."

He handed it over.

I took with left hand.

Shoulder complained less.

"Bench?" he asked.

"Maybe."

"Here would be ideal."

Rusk from bench said, "For what?"

Dask began.

"Retired short-run line quietener, passive brass plate, likely split leaf internal but older type, intended to suppress echo or false tone on short copper signaling runs while unfortunately reducing weak true tones as well."

Rusk kept working.

"So bad bell helper."

Dask looked pained.

"That is incomplete."

"Still understood."

I liked Rusk.

Greyhook had its own test bench for retired signal hardware.

Of course.

Wind towers used short copper runs from weighted strip frames to local click boxes.

Not magic maybe.

Not only magic.

Mostly mechanics and line resonance.

Rusk said bench belonged yard foreman, not him.

Foreman **Tala Venn** was currently up tower three swearing at west vane.

"If she comes down not mad, ask."

"If mad?"

"Ask tomorrow."

Good system.

Weather hold board changed at first evening bell.

Aven Ro crossed terrace shouting before sign even got chalk.

"North Reach still held! West strip disagrees! Tower one green, tower two green, tower three red twice in quarter bell! No one gets creative!"

A freight man shouted, "What if we're already creative?"

"Then be creative indoors!"

She kept walking.

Excellent management.

Vessa checked route board.

"Morning earliest."

No frustration in voice.

Just fact.

I had learned this crew traveled by fact more than desire.

Useful.

Rusk opened resin tin.

Smelled like pine and hot stone.

Filled tooth marks with narrow bone spatula.

Wrapped deepest section in thin dark fiber tape soaked with resin.

Not pretty.

Strong-looking.

"Will wrap change flex?" Dask asked.

Rusk: "Tiny."

"How tiny?"

"Tiny enough I'm not measuring for you."

Dask inhaled through nose.

Sori sat beside me.

"He's growing."

"Painfully."

"Like fungus."

Dask looked over.

"I can hear you."

"Good."

Crew normal.

That helped.

No one had asked me to demonstrate hound technique.

No one wanted locked Greg back out for entertainment.

Good people.

Maybe.

Tala Venn came down tower three near second bell.

Small woman.

Maybe fifty.

Hair braided under leather cap.

One eye watering from wind.

She was absolutely mad.

She kicked tower stair bottom.

"West vane is lying."

Rusk said, "Vane can't lie."

"Then whoever set lower weight is lying through vane."

She saw us.

"Survey?"

Vessa nodded.

"Held north."

"I know. Everyone knows because Aven has lungs."

Aven somewhere above shouted something unintelligible.

Tala pointed upward.

"See."

I waited.

Dask did not.

"We have retired short-run line quietener and would like bench-only comparison if yard permits."

Tala stared.

Then at package.

Then at me.

"Yours?"

"Yes."

"Live line?"

"No."

"Good, because I would hit you with it."

Reasonable.

She took maintenance card.

Read.

"Old West Locks pattern."

"Likely," Dask said.

"Not likely. Stamp says West Locks."

Dask leaned.

There was tiny district mark under grease stain.

He looked betrayed by own eyesight.

Tala enjoyed this.

"Bench three. Short copper. Mechanical tone source. No field light. No active relay. We can see if plate still does basic bad-bell-helper job."

Rusk smiled without looking up.

Dask whispered, "It is not called that."

I said, "It is now."

Bench three sat inside second shed.

Simple enough.

Two upright pegs.

Copper line between.

Small striker box on one end.

Listening plate on other.

A second branch with adjustable slack and old echo loop.

Tala explained.

Normal strike made one clean click at plate.

Echo loop could create weaker delayed second click.

Quietener inserted between two short leads.

No magic.

No live signaling.

No stakes beyond curiosity.

Exactly right.

I unwrapped brass plate.

First time as owner.

Heavy for size.

Three notches.

Black retirement slash faint.

Spring leaf inside slit visible when tilted.

Dask wanted to touch.

Did not ask.

I looked at him.

He sighed.

"May I?"

"After first run."

"Fine."

Growth under oppression.

Tala ran baseline.

CLACK.

Then weaker tick.

Clear enough.

She adjusted slack.

Again.

CLACK.

Tick.

"Echo deliberately exaggerated," she said. "Real line messier."

Greg understood.

We inserted quietener.

No drama.

No glow.

No hum.

Tala struck.

Clack.

Nothing obvious after.

Dask leaned toward plate.

"Again."

Tala: "You say please to my bench."

He blinked.

"Please."

Again.

Clack.

Tiny delayed sound maybe.

Much less.

There.

It worked.

At least on toy problem designed to show exact use.

Useful.

Known.

Then Tala reduced main strike strength.

"Now downside."

Baseline weak strike without quietener.

Click.

Echo softer.

With quietener:

Tick.

Barely.

Dask frowned.

I did too.

Tala nodded.

"There. It doesn't know truth. It knows shape and strength."

Good line.

Not magic wisdom.

Engineering.

That was why thing was dangerous.

It could not distinguish false from important.

Neither could lots of people.

I liked it more.

Which was bad.

"One more," I said.

Tala looked.

"Why?"

"Different echo delay. Same main strength."

She nodded.

Good question apparently.

Adjusted branch.

Longer delay.

Baseline gave clean main + later weak tick.

Quietener damped later tick less than short-delay echo.

Interesting.

Dask started speaking fast.

"Frequency or phase sensitivity maybe, or mechanical settling time, possibly leaf preload relation, if we vary line tension and delay independently we'd need grid, perhaps twelve runs minimum, preferably twenty-four."

Tala held up hand.

"No."

He stopped.

"Why?"

"Because my bench is for work. You got answer. Plate functions. Downside functions. Go away."

I wrapped quietener.

"Thank you."

"You bought a problem."

"Yes."

"Good. Most interesting tools are."

There.

Collector logic.

Not power.

Problem with shape.

Back outside, Rusk had crutch hanging under roof beam to cure.

"One hour."

Shoulder had stiffened while sitting.

I stood carefully.

Left crutch only plus wall hand.

Bad idea for travel.

Fine for three steps.

Sori offered arm.

I took it.

No speech.

Small recalibration.

Greyhook evening market was mostly workers selling worker things.

Wind goggles.

Leather tie loops.

Weighted cloak hems.

Hook gloves with reinforced palms.

Dried meat.

Tiny bottles of eye oil.

One table of bent signal vanes sold as wall decoration to people with questionable taste.

I wanted one.

Did not buy.

Fifteen copper.

Vale twenty-three.

Money not crisis.

Still money.

I bought nothing.

Look at me.

Growth.

Kel did buy a weighted scarf.

Sori mocked him until wind hit her face on upper terrace.

Then she asked where seller was.

Kel refused to tell for almost five minutes.

Justice.

At third bell, Greyhook performed wind check.

All three towers visible from yard.

Huge slatted arms angled into wind.

Weighted cloth strips hung from side booms.

Tower one green flag.

Tower two green.

Tower three red.

Then green.

Aven watched through brass tube.

"Need half bell agreement."

People groaned.

Not us.

We had bunks.

I had repaired crutch soon.

Weather could be weather.

Rusk returned right crutch after cure.

Resin dark around tooth grooves.

Thin reinforcement wrap maybe four inches long.

He handed it to me.

"Test here."

I did.

Plant.

Weight.

Forward.

Back.

Small twist.

No creak.

No give.

Grip same.

Flex maybe different by amount Dask would ruin evening trying to name.

"Feels good."

Rusk: "Feels sound?"

I corrected.

"Feels sound."

"Good. Don't hit dogs for two days."

"Planning not to."

"Plans attract dogs."

Maybe true.

Vessa appeared with route update.

"Window possibly dawn. Aven wants everyone ready first bell. If towers disagree, we wait. If they agree half bell, we cross immediately."

"What is cross?"

"Greyhook crown to North Reach shelf. About one and three-quarter miles exposed. Anchor chain every thirty paces. Two wind shelters. One stair descent. No wagons. Mule line separate lower shelf."

I looked shoulder.

She saw.

"Can you do it if window opens?"

Good question.

Not can you force it.

Can you do it.

"Probably. Need right shoulder reassess morning. Chain requirement?"

"No hand-on-chain if green window. Chain is emergency only."

Better.

"Then probably yes."

"If probably becomes no, say no."

"Yes."

There.

Normal Greg.

No performance.

Night bunks were in long stone room built into ridge.

Wind thumped roof anyway.

Dask wanted to write bench results into personal notes.

I let him copy maintenance card observations but kept ownership notes myself.

New artifact entry mentally:

Line quietener.

Works on short copper bench.

Reduces short-delay echo strongly.

Reduces weak true strike too.

Longer-delay echo damped less in one bench condition.

No claim beyond bench.

No live use.

No magic interaction known.

Useful.

Dangerous.

Mine.

That last word felt good.

Collection growing.

Not because I needed to fill slots.

Because objects had stories and constraints and ways they could change decisions.

Holdfast waited Carrow.

Retreat oval waited Merecross.

Rest stone.

Shade unit.

Step Keeper.

Now this.

Most of them I barely understood.

Excellent.

Sori lay on bunk above me.

"You smiling at brass?"

"No."

"You're smiling."

"Shoulder pain."

"Looks romantic."

"Go to sleep."

"Customer."

"Don't start."

She laughed.

Wind hit wall.

Stone room shuddered tiny amount.

Nobody cared.

I did.

New place.

New rules.

Tomorrow maybe we crossed exposed crown where wind itself decided whether road existed.

Tonight I had one repaired crutch, one sore shoulder, one dangerous little brass plate, fifteen copper, twenty-three copper of Vale, and no reason to become more than that.

Repairman.

Not because I fixed crutch.

Rusk did.

Not because I fixed quietener.

Didn't need fixing.

Because day had been about keeping useful things useful.

Body.

Equipment.

Judgment.

Even restraint.

Turns out maintenance was adventure too.

Annoying.
# CHAPTER 399

## THE CROSSER

Tower three went green before breakfast.

Nobody trusted it.

Reasonable.

Aven Ro stood under the route board with a cup in one hand and her coat snapping around her knees.

"One green. Two green. Three green. Clock starts now. Nobody celebrates."

Dask looked offended.

"I wasn't going to celebrate."

"Good. Keep doing that."

Greyhook morning had apparently begun angry.

I liked consistency.

My shoulder liked nothing.

Better than yesterday.

Not good.

I tested it beside the bunkhouse while the tower crews watched their weighted strips.

Forward lift.

Fine until high.

Side lift.

Still complained.

Grip.

Sore, functional.

Right crutch.

Plant.

Weight.

Twist.

The dark resin marks and narrow reinforcement wrap held.

No creak.

No give.

Good.

Vessa watched from three paces away.

"Probably?"

"Still probably."

"Any worse?"

"No."

"Any numbness?"

"No."

"Then probably can go."

There.

Not heroic.

Medical science.

Probably.

Aven shouted from board.

"Quarter bell!"

The three strips stayed green.

Wind moved through Greyhook hard enough to make every hanging chain talk.

Not loud exactly.

Constant.

Iron against iron.

Cloth snapping.

Wood knocking.

People raising voices because the ridge stole half of every sentence.

Kel came out wearing the weighted scarf he'd bought yesterday.

Sori pointed.

"Still stupid."

A gust hit her sideways.

She caught the wall.

"Where was the seller?"

Kel smiled.

"Market closed."

"I hate you."

"No you don't."

"Currently flexible."

Dask had tied his pencils to his coat.

Individually.

Three little cords.

I stared.

He noticed.

"Wind."

"I know what wind is."

"Then why are you looking?"

"I'm learning what fear looks like in a pencil."

Maro laughed into his sleeve.

Vessa said, "Load check."

We did.

My bag sat close against body.

Quietener wrapped inside with maintenance card and two short copper leads.

Tavi's striped rock farther down.

Knife.

Water.

Food.

Nothing loose.

No stupid decorative vane.

Regret.

Aven shouted again.

"Half bell! Window open!"

Everything changed quickly.

Not panic.

Work.

A gate on the north stair opened.

Two freight crews moved first toward the lower mule shelf.

Our cases had already been transferred to that line before dawn.

We carried only personal load and one compact record case Sori refused to surrender.

Vessa checked each of us.

"Crown to shelter one. Shelter one to stair. Stair to shelter two. Shelter two to north gate. Nobody races the window. If red call comes, nearest shelter. If chain bell rings, clip if you have clip, hold if you don't. Greg?"

"No clip."

"Emergency chain with both hands if stopped."

I looked at crutches.

"That would be exciting."

"Avoid excitement."

"Plan already established."

Aven handed us six green cloth tags.

"Tie visible. North gate counts tags, not faces. If you lose one, tell them before they decide the wind ate you."

I tied mine to bag strap.

Sori tied Dask's because his knot was apparently insulting.

"It was secure," he said.

"It was a measurement knot."

"That's not a thing."

"It looked like one."

We climbed to crown.

Then Greyhook ended.

Not literally.

Emotionally.

The ridge ahead had no interest in people.

North Reach ran like a narrow back of red-black stone between two enormous drops.

West side fell into pale broken country full of dry gullies and low cloud shadow.

East side dropped sharper into a green-gray basin I couldn't see the bottom of.

The maintained path was maybe eight feet wide at first.

Sometimes twelve.

Sometimes five.

Anchor posts stood every thirty paces or so, iron sunk into stone, heavy chain sagging between them at knee to waist height depending ground.

Not a railing.

Too low and too far from path in places.

Emergency infrastructure.

Something to reach if walking stopped being walking.

Wind shelters looked tiny from crown.

Stone boxes with one side open away from prevailing gust.

One maybe half mile out.

Second beyond stair.

North gate invisible.

I had crossed worse.

First life.

Different body.

Different world.

That fact used to annoy me.

Now it was just accounting.

Vessa said, "Maro first. Kel second. Greg center. Sori. Dask. Me rear. Ten paces spacing until shelter one."

Nobody argued.

We crossed.

First twenty paces were easy.

Of course.

The wind wanted confidence before collecting tax.

Crutch tips clicked against stone.

Right.

Left.

Foot.

Not actually right-left-foot.

My body knew sequence better than language did.

Two points ahead.

One behind.

Weight centered low.

Do not let upper body chase gust.

Let shoulders move a little.

Keep pelvis boring.

Boring pelvis survived weather.

That was probably not a proverb.

Could be.

At forty paces first real gust hit from west.

Not push.

Impact.

My coat flattened against side.

Bag tugged.

Right crutch unloaded for half heartbeat.

I let it.

Didn't snatch for ground.

Left crutch and right foot held triangle.

Then right tip came down again.

There.

Current body.

Current competence.

Nobody said anything.

Good.

Maro raised fist ahead.

Stop.

We stopped.

Not because danger.

Because a freight line below was moving.

Far under west lip, three mules walked narrow shelf with linked cases between handlers.

Wind carried no hoof sound up.

Made them look fake.

Tiny animals moving without noise.

Dask behind me said something.

Wind stole all of it.

I turned.

"What?"

He shouted.

Still nothing.

Sori yelled, "HE SAID THE WEST VANE MOVED!"

I looked back toward Greyhook.

One tower arm shifted.

Green strips stayed green.

Fine.

Dask shouted again.

Sori shouted, "HE KNOWS!"

This system was excellent.

We moved.

Path narrowed.

Six feet.

Then five.

Chain closer on west side.

I hated chain being west side.

If gust pushed east, chain was behind direction of travel.

Probably intentional for prevailing wind.

Today wind mostly west.

Fine.

Mostly was a dangerous word.

Shelter one came after enough walking that shoulder had started warming rather than hurting.

Good sign.

We entered one at a time.

Inside, silence hit almost as hard as wind outside.

Not true silence.

Stone hummed.

But conversation returned.

Kel said, "I can't hear myself think out there."

Dask said, "I can."

Sori: "Tragic."

Vessa checked time strip nailed inside shelter.

Simple weighted ribbon protected by glass.

"Window still green. Five minutes water."

I drank.

Shoulder assessment.

Warm.

Not worse.

Palm okay.

Right crutch wrap still sound.

Maro leaned against back wall.

"Next section worse."

"Encouraging," I said.

"You want lie?"

"Depends quality."

"Next section has pastries."

"Terrible."

"I don't practice."

Outside, chain bell rang once.

Everyone looked.

Vessa was already at opening.

Second ring.

Not alarm pattern.

Aven had explained.

Two isolated rings meant gust front passing Greyhook crown.

Three fast meant stop and shelter.

Continuous meant clip or hold.

We waited.

No third.

Vessa watched dust farther west.

A brown sheet moved across lower gullies.

Not toward us exactly.

Parallel.

"Two minutes," she said.

Nobody complained.

There.

Weather wasn't plot.

Weather was schedule.

We left.

Next section had no pastries.

Maro had lied.

Path angled down along east face.

Wind changed because ridge changed it.

Instead of steady west pressure, gusts curled upward.

That was worse.

Crutch tips got light without warning.

Not sliding.

Unweighting.

I shortened stride.

Crutch.

Crutch.

Foot.

Pause when needed.

Kel ahead turned once.

I gave thumbs-up.

He kept going.

No babysitting.

Good.

At first stair, Vessa changed order.

"Greg behind Kel. Sori behind Greg. Maro takes bottom."

Stone stair cut twenty-three steps down across exposed face.

Chain at outer edge.

Inner wall shoulder-high first half, knee-high second.

Wonderful.

I looked.

Old Greg brain offered six ways to descend quickly.

Current shoulder rejected four.

Current body rejected another.

One remained.

Fine.

"Backward?" Kel asked.

"Sideways."

I turned toward wall.

Right foot down.

Left crutch lower step.

Right crutch same level as foot until weight transferred.

Then down.

Slow.

Stable.

Wind shoved coat against wall.

Useful for once.

Step nine.

Ten.

Eleven.

Shoulder complained.

Not dangerous.

Twelve.

Thirteen.

A gust hit upward.

Right crutch tip skipped half inch.

Stopped against stair lip.

My body froze exactly long enough.

No more.

Sori behind said nothing.

Good.

I reset.

Continued.

At bottom Maro waited.

"Fine?"

"Yes."

"Actually?"

I rolled shoulder once.

"Six breaths."

Vessa heard from above.

"Take ten."

"Abuse of authority."

"Nine now."

I shut up.

Ten breaths.

There.

Patient survived becoming crosser.

We moved.

Second shelter was smaller.

Also occupied.

Two Roads workers sat inside with a coil of bright orange rope between them and a broken wind-strip frame on floor.

One woman had nose packed with cloth from a bleed.

The other man was eating something that smelled aggressively of onion.

"Room," woman said.

We squeezed.

Eight people in stone box built for maybe six.

Dask immediately looked at broken frame.

Then looked at owner.

Progress.

"May I?"

Woman followed his eyes.

"No."

"Okay."

More progress.

She pointed at my repaired crutch.

"Dog?"

Regional gossip again.

"Yes."

"Three Posts?"

"Unfortunately."

Onion man said, "Heard you killed six."

"Killed none."

"Heard eight."

"Still none."

"That's less interesting."

"For hounds, better."

Woman snorted and immediately regretted it because nose.

"Fuck."

Sori handed her clean cloth.

"Thanks."

Vessa asked, "North section?"

Woman became work again.

"Crosswind stronger after marker forty. Not red. Tower call still green. One loose chain between fifty-two and fifty-three, flagged blue. Don't use it. North gate knows."

"Any debris?"

"Small grit. Nothing with ambition."

Good phrase.

I kept it.

A bell rang outside.

One.

Pause.

One.

Not pattern.

Dask counted anyway.

Of course.

Road woman said, "Greyhook crown settling. You're fine."

Vessa waited another minute.

Then we went.

North section widened briefly.

That was trap emotionally.

Because wider path meant stronger wind.

Nothing broke it.

Sound disappeared almost completely.

Not quiet.

Pressure.

Air roaring so evenly it became absence.

I could see Kel's coat snap and hear almost none of it.

Sori's mouth moved once.

No sound.

She stopped trying.

Good.

We communicated by hands.

Maro fist.

Stop.

Palm low.

Crouch slightly.

Point west.

Gust.

We waited.

Dust and tiny stone grains skittered across path.

One hit cheek.

Then another.

Nothing with ambition.

Accurate.

Maro dropped hand.

Move.

At marker forty-seven, wind shifted east for three breaths.

That was interesting.

Not magical necessarily.

Terrain.

Air.

Ridge.

Dask's head turned hard.

I saw question happen.

He didn't stop.

Also progress.

Marker fifty-two had blue cloth tied around chain.

Loose section sagged lower than others.

We stayed inner path.

No touch.

Marker fifty-four.

Fifty-five.

Then the wind stopped.

Completely.

Everyone stopped too.

Not because order.

Because wrong.

My coat fell against body.

Kel's weighted scarf hung dead.

Dust dropped.

For maybe two breaths North Reach became still.

Not sheltered.

Still.

I felt skin tighten.

Dask looked at Vessa.

Maro looked at sky.

Vessa raised fist.

Hold.

No bells.

No tower signal visible this far.

Three breaths.

Four.

Then wind returned from west with a slap.

We leaned.

Normal.

Vessa pointed forward.

Move.

Good.

No investigation in middle of exposed ridge.

That was how people died while being curious.

North gate appeared after marker sixty.

Stone wall across widened shelf.

Low building.

Two wind masts.

Three people waving us in.

We crossed final stretch.

My shoulder hurt now.

Not injured-new.

Used.

Palm sore.

Breathing harder.

Still controlled.

North gate worker counted green tags before faces.

"Six!"

Vessa answered, "Six!"

Gate shut behind us.

Not dramatic.

Wood and iron.

Then I was inside lee wall and suddenly heard everyone again.

Dask said, "At marker fifty-five the wind velocity approached zero for approximately four breaths."

Sori said, "Hello to you too."

"It did."

"We survived. Say hello first."

He looked at me.

"Hello."

"Wrong person."

I sat on first available bench.

"Acceptable effort."

Vessa checked me.

"Shoulder?"

"Used. Not worse in a new way."

"Hand?"

"Sore."

"Crutch?"

I planted right one twice.

Solid.

"Rusk wins."

Kel pulled off weighted scarf.

Sori held hand out.

He stared.

"What?"

"I want to try it."

"You called it stupid."

"I contain growth."

He gave it to her.

North gate worker came over.

Older man, broad face, missing half an eyebrow.

"Survey?"

Vessa showed papers.

He read.

"Merecross. Long way."

"Getting longer."

"That's roads."

He pointed north.

"Your cases come mule shelf in maybe an hour. North Reach Station is down slope, not up. Don't follow the tower road unless you want weather people yelling at you."

"Route beyond?"

"Station will brief."

Dask said, "Was the still-air interval at marker fifty-five expected?"

Worker's face changed a little.

Not fear.

Recognition.

"You got one?"

"Approximately four breaths."

"Huh."

"What is it?"

"Usually nothing."

I hated usually.

Pella had taught me that.

Worker scratched missing eyebrow side.

"Reach gets dead pockets. Wind folds wrong around stone. Most are one breath, two. Four's longer. Tower crews record them."

"Magical?" Dask asked.

"Weather."

"That doesn't answer."

"It answers enough for breakfast."

I liked him.

Vessa said, "Name?"

"Holl Renn."

Dask turned.

Holl looked at him.

"No relation that I know."

"I hadn't asked yet."

"You turned around."

Dask closed mouth.

Excellent.

We waited for cases.

North side of Reach was not what I'd expected.

I hadn't expected anything specific.

Still.

Greyhook's dry red ridge fell away into a high basin full of dark grass and white stone ribs.

Not marsh.

Not forest.

Open rolling country.

Wind moved across grass in huge visible sheets.

Far north, something silver cut horizontally across basin.

River maybe.

Road definitely.

And beyond that, low blue hills layered into distance.

More world.

There it was again.

That feeling.

Carrow existed behind me.

Merecross behind that.

Bell Ford.

Alder Basin.

West Locks.

Three Posts.

Lark Spur.

Greyhook.

Names accumulating.

Not replacing home.

Adding to map inside me.

I had wanted a door that didn't lead home before dinner.

Apparently the world had taken that personally.

The mule cases arrived forty-eight minutes later.

Dask knew because of course he did.

No damage.

One seal dusty.

Sori checked custody.

Kel checked straps.

Vessa got station directions.

We descended.

North Reach Station sat half mile below gate behind a long white stone windbreak.

Bigger than Three Posts.

Smaller than Lark Spur.

Two bunkhouses.

Stable.

Signal mast.

Survey office.

Public cookhouse.

And something I had not seen in days.

A proper bath sign.

I stopped.

Maro nearly walked into me.

"What?"

I pointed.

He followed finger.

"Bath?"

"Bath."

"You've seen bath."

"Not recently enough."

Sori came beside us.

"Assignment covers?"

Vessa, ahead, didn't turn.

"Basic wash only. Hot soak personal."

There.

Economy returned.

I looked at sign.

**BASIC WASH - ASSIGNMENT / ROAD CREW**

**HOT BASIN - 1C**

One copper.

I had fifteen.

Vale had twenty-three of my future.

My shoulder hurt.

My hand hurt.

I had crossed a wind ridge on crutches.

This was not existential.

This was value.

I said, "I'm buying the bath."

Sori looked at me.

"Immediately?"

"Before anyone invents work."

Vessa finally turned.

"Briefing first."

"Cruel."

"Then bath."

Acceptable.

Inside survey office, station lead laid map on table.

Her name was **Ira Fen**.

Thin woman with silver hair cut to chin and ink on three fingers.

She spoke like every sentence had already been edited once before leaving her mouth.

"You crossed during a clean window?"

Vessa said, "Mostly. Four-breath dead pocket near fifty-five."

Ira wrote that without reaction.

"Common enough. Long enough to log."

Dask visibly relaxed because someone had finally used acceptable wording.

Ira continued.

"Your north assignment changes here. Merecross requested observational continuity through North Reach, then discretion for extension if regional conditions justify. They do."

There.

Something moved.

Not wind.

Story.

Vessa leaned over map.

"What conditions?"

Ira tapped three places.

"False tones at West Locks. Three Posts arm drift. Greyhook dead pockets longer than seasonal average. North basin has a different problem."

Dask inhaled.

Ira looked at him.

"Don't connect them yet."

He exhaled.

Good woman.

She tapped silver line I'd seen from gate.

"This is the **Lume River**. North road crosses at **White Span**. For four mornings, the river has reflected sunrise from the wrong direction."

Silence.

Ira added, "Only for several minutes. Physical sun remains east. Reflection appears west-facing on calm water. No heat change. No known navigation effect. Local ferrymen hate it."

I looked at map.

New problem.

Different grammar.

Good.

"How far?" Vessa asked.

"White Span twelve miles by road. Halfway settlement at **Kettle Vale**. You can make Kettle Vale tomorrow if you leave first bell. White Span day after."

There.

Not home.

Farther.

Ira said, "You have two choices. Remain here one day for North Reach observations, or continue under extension and take the basin route."

Vessa looked at crew.

Not just me.

Good.

Kel shrugged first.

"Road's open."

Maro said, "I haven't seen Lume in years."

Sori looked at Vessa.

"Custody okay if station stamps extension."

Dask said nothing.

That was suspicious.

Then: "I would like to observe the river."

Of course.

Vessa looked at me.

Shoulder sore.

Hand sore.

Fifteen copper.

One bath waiting.

Home farther south than it had ever been in this life.

"Greg?"

I looked at map.

Kettle Vale.

White Span.

Lume River.

Wrong sunrise.

Then north beyond it.

"Bath first," I said.

Vessa's mouth twitched.

"Then?"

"Then north."

There.

Crosser.

Apparently one ridge wasn't enough.
# CHAPTER 400

## THE SOJOURNER

I paid one copper for hot water.

Best purchase of expedition.

Possibly best artifact too.

Nobody liked that comparison.

North Reach bathhouse had four stone basins separated by waist-high walls, one cold channel, one hot channel, and a woman at desk who looked capable of denying civilization to anyone who annoyed her.

I gave her copper.

She bit it.

Normal.

"Half bell."

"Can I buy another half?"

"After first half."

"Excellent system."

She stared.

I stopped talking.

Also excellent system.

Hot water reached shoulder and every muscle in body immediately filed complaint.

There.

That was the problem with being busy.

Body waited until safe before becoming dramatic.

Right shoulder loosened slowly.

Palm stopped feeling like somebody had packed it with gravel.

Forearm still sore.

Nothing healed.

Everything became less stupid.

I sank lower.

First life had baths too.

Better ones sometimes.

Worse ones often.

Hot spring under ruined keep.

Copper tub in mountain inn.

One terrible adventurer bath where three men argued about whose blood clogged drain.

This was better because nobody was dying.

Also I was nineteen.

Again.

Still weird.

Less weird than before.

I thought of Carrow.

Cala's kitchen.

Tavi's noise.

Lyssa.

Theatre.

Vale.

My chest did small thing.

Not pain.

Pull.

Home.

Then I thought of map upstairs.

Kettle Vale.

White Span.

Lume River.

Wrong sunrise.

Pull opposite direction.

Interesting.

Maybe belonging was not rope.

Maybe it was weight.

Home could pull without preventing movement.

I liked that better.

Bath woman knocked wood against stone partition.

"Five minutes."

Cruel.

I stood carefully.

Shoulder better.

Still there.

Good.

I did not buy second half.

One copper had done job.

There.

Restraint.

Cash fourteen.

Vale twenty-three.

Still not dying.

I dressed and returned to Survey office smelling less like hound, marsh, wind, and bad decisions.

Sori noticed first.

"You look human."

"Expensive."

"One copper."

"Exactly."

Dask looked at shoulder.

"Range improved?"

"Do not turn bath into test protocol."

"I wasn't."

"You were halfway there."

He considered.

"Maybe."

Growth.

Ira Fen had extension papers ready.

Three sheets.

One station stamp.

One regional seal.

One line I actually cared about.

**OBSERVATIONAL CONTINUITY AUTHORIZED THROUGH WHITE SPAN / LUME RIVER.**

Vessa read everything.

Sori read everything again because that was Sori.

Dask tried to read over shoulder.

Sori moved page three inches away.

He moved with it.

She moved again.

He stopped.

"I'm not touching."

"You're breathing on custody."

"Air is not custody interference."

"Keep arguing and it becomes one."

Ira stamped page.

"Food through Kettle Vale covered. Public lodging covered if station bunks unavailable. White Span local boats are not automatically covered unless survey use is authorized there. Personal purchases remain personal."

Greg economy loved sentences like that.

Vessa asked, "Route conditions?"

Ira tapped map.

"North basin road dry. Wind moderate. Two long grades. One white-stone causeway across lower grass floodplain. No weather hold. Kettle Vale has well, station desk, inn, repair stable, market on alternating days. Today is not market day."

Damn.

Ira continued.

"White Span road beyond Vale is open. River crews want outside witnesses at dawn if reflection repeats. That means you need Kettle Vale tonight. Leave within half bell."

There.

Bath then north.

Promise kept.

We packed.

Nothing dramatic.

That was becoming its own pleasure.

Kel checked straps.

Sori sealed papers.

Dask tied pencils again even though wind inside basin looked less violent.

Maro stood outside looking north like person who had done this before and forgotten enough to enjoy it again.

Vessa counted people.

Six.

Always six.

I checked bag.

Quietener.

Tavi rock.

Knife.

Food.

Water.

Paper.

Fourteen copper.

No oval.

Artifacts had geography now.

Some home.

Some Merecross.

Some with me.

Collection becoming map too.

We left North Reach Station before second bell.

High basin swallowed us differently than ridge.

Wind still existed, but no longer had teeth.

Dark grass bent in huge sheets from west to east.

White stone ribs rose from ground every few hundred paces like backs of buried animals.

Road was pale hardpack with black drainage cuts.

Long sightlines.

Nothing could hide unless it tried very hard.

I liked it immediately.

Then disliked it after forty minutes because long sightlines made distance rude.

You could see hill forever before reaching it.

Maro said, "That one is first grade."

I looked at hill.

"That one?"

"Yes."

"We've been walking toward it since birth."

"Maybe longer."

Dask said, "Approximately forty-three minutes."

Sori groaned.

"Nobody asked."

"Greg implied duration."

"Greg implied suffering."

"Those can overlap."

Hard to argue.

First grade climbed steadily.

Not steep.

Worse.

Steady meant no excuse to stop.

Shoulder warmed, then complained.

Palm okay.

Right crutch repair held.

At top Vessa gave five breaths without me asking.

I took eight.

Nobody counted except Dask.

He did not say number.

Actual growth.

From ridge crest we saw Lume River clearly for first time.

Silver line far north.

Too far for water detail.

Wide enough to matter.

White Span itself invisible.

Kettle Vale somewhere lower, hidden behind rolling grass and stone.

I stood there longer than needed.

Not because magic.

Scale.

Carrow had become small in imagination behind me.

Not less important.

Just geographically small.

Different.

In first life I had crossed kingdoms.

This should not impress me.

It did.

Second life made distance personal again.

Maybe because there were people waiting behind it now.

First life at nineteen had mostly wanted away.

Current nineteen had something to return to.

That made north feel farther.

And better.

Maro said, "You okay?"

"Yes."

"You're staring."

"River."

"Still there."

"Good."

We descended.

At lower grass floodplain road became causeway.

White stone blocks, three feet above surrounding dark grass.

Grass looked solid until wind moved it and revealed water shining beneath.

Floodplain.

Not marsh exactly.

Seasonal sheet water hidden under grass roots.

Causeway had gaps every fifty paces with narrow bridges over flow cuts.

No rails.

Because apparently this region hated decorative safety.

Kel said, "Watch right edge. Some stones undercut."

Local sign agreed.

**KEEP CENTER / WHITE MARKS SAFE / BLUE MARKS UNDER REVIEW**

Blue paint appeared every so often.

Dask loved system.

"Clear visual coding."

Sori said, "Please marry road."

"Road has no legal personhood."

"Coward."

Halfway across, grass to east moved wrong.

Not wind.

Something long traveled beneath.

We all saw.

Maro stopped.

Shape maybe ten feet.

Could be water channel.

Then head surfaced.

Pale.

Flat.

Two dark side fins.

Mud sailer maybe.

There.

The bridge animal again? Not same animal. Too far.

Species perhaps.

Creature surfaced once, breathed with ugly wet cough, then vanished.

Dask whispered, "That was likely a mud sailer."

Maro: "Likely."

"Could we stop?"

Vessa: "No."

"For thirty seconds?"

"No."

"Ten?"

"Walk."

He walked.

Greg understood pain.

I looked anyway while moving.

Nothing returned.

Good.

No monster fight.

Just animal.

Road after causeway climbed second grade.

Shorter.

Steeper.

My shoulder disliked more.

I stopped once.

Ten breaths.

Asked before world asked for me.

There.

Smart.

At top Kel offered to take bag.

I almost said no.

Then checked shoulder.

"Twenty minutes."

He took it.

No ceremony.

Sori saw.

Said nothing.

Good.

Locked Greg had turned people into variables.

Normal Greg could let variable carry bag.

Maybe that was healthy.

Kel wore bag badly.

Too high.

I endured for three minutes.

"Lower strap."

He adjusted.

"More."

Adjusted.

"There."

"You're difficult."

"I'm injured, not dead."

"Debatable."

Normal crew.

Road crossed little stone marker field near afternoon.

Dozens of waist-high white pillars on both sides.

Each had shallow bowl carved top.

Most empty.

Some held water despite no rain.

Dask slowed.

Maro said, "Old wind wells."

"What do they do?" I asked.

"Collect condensation when nights cool. Travelers used to drink."

"Safe?"

"Not now. Birds shit in them."

Magic defeated by bird.

Excellent.

One bowl had tiny silver shimmer around edge.

I looked.

Kept walking.

Not everything needed investigation.

This was becoming real skill.

Late afternoon road finally dropped.

Kettle Vale appeared all at once.

Not valley exactly.

Bowl between white stone ridges.

Maybe forty buildings.

More than Lark Spur.

Less than Carrow.

Roofs dark slate.

Several round steam vents.

One tall black chimney.

Fields in terraces.

Roads converging from east and north.

And kettles.

Actually kettles.

Huge iron ones outside buildings, some big enough to bathe horse.

I stopped.

"Why?"

Maro smiled.

"You'll like this."

"That worries me."

We entered under stone arch painted:

**KETTLE VALE / HOT SPRINGS, BREWERS, ROAD REST**

There.

Of course.

Natural hot water.

Brewer town.

Road stop.

Name literal enough.

Smell hit next.

Mineral water.

Malt.

Smoke.

Bread.

I forgave region immediately.

Station desk occupied front room of inn called **The Copper Kettle**.

Too obvious.

Perfect.

Desk clerk was broad man named **Orren Pike**, beard braided in two little ropes, voice too formal for room.

"Good afternoon. Survey travelers under regional extension?"

Vessa showed papers.

"Yes. Six."

"We have been informed of your likely arrival. Accommodations are available in rear annex. Evening meal covered under road assignment. Bathing is not included because our communal spring is separately operated."

I looked at Vessa.

She said, "You already bought one."

Cruel again.

Orren continued like tax record.

"White Span departure recommended before first bell. Dawn reflection, if it repeats, begins shortly after first direct light upon western bank. Ferrymaster requests observers positioned before sunrise. Road distance approximately six miles."

Dask asked, "Duration of prior reflections?"

Orren consulted note.

"Morning one: about six minutes. Morning two: eight or nine. Morning three: seven. Morning four: five. Times are local estimates except morning four, which was clocked at five minutes and twenty breaths by bridge assistant."

Good.

Better evidence already.

"Any effect on people?" Vessa asked.

"None reported."

"Boats?"

"None reported."

"Fish?"

Orren paused.

"One ferryman claims fish rise toward false light. Second ferryman says first ferryman lies when sober. I cannot classify."

I liked Orren too.

Sori said, "Market?"

Orren looked at her.

"Tomorrow afternoon."

I suffered quietly.

Vessa said, "Tomorrow is not today."

"I know."

"Good."

We got rear annex.

Six bunks.

Again.

No argument this time.

Luxury.

Kel returned my bag after exactly twenty-three minutes.

I did not ask how he knew.

Dask did.

Of course.

Shoulder felt better after unload.

Not healed.

Maybe fifty percent angry instead of seventy.

Useful scale invented entirely from mood.

Evening meal was thick barley stew, dark bread, pickled onions.

Good.

Dask ate onions individually because apparently food had measurement protocol too.

Sori watched him for one minute.

"Why?"

"I like them separately."

There.

Not technical.

Human.

She accepted.

After food Vessa assigned dawn plan.

Leave Kettle Vale before first bell.

Reach White Span before sunrise.

Maro river/terrain.

Dask instruments.

Sori records/custody.

Kel transport/logistics.

Greg witness log with Ira's observation framing.

No special Greg role.

Good.

I asked, "Can I see bridge before dawn without standing on bridge?"

Maro said, "West bank has rise above span. Best view."

"Good."

Dask asked, "Could quietener have any relevance?"

There.

Vessa looked at me.

I looked at wrapped object.

"No evidence. Different system. Leave packed unless local owner asks about it for separate reason."

Dask nodded.

No fight.

Growth.

We had one hour before sleep.

I walked outside.

Kettle Vale at night steamed.

Literally.

Warm vapor rose from drainage channels along road.

People sat on stone benches with cups.

Brewers rolled barrels.

Someone sang badly in building nearby.

Children chased each other between kettles until woman yelled at them not to die in boiling water.

Lived in.

Far from home.

And ordinary.

There.

That was the thing.

Adventure was not constant danger.

It was breakfast somewhere you didn't know yesterday.

A bath purchased because shoulder hurt.

A road with strange grass.

A town that smelled like malt.

A river tomorrow reflecting wrong sun.

And people back home continuing without me.

I wondered what Tavi had done today.

Probably something loud.

Cala probably worked.

Lyssa probably had own day entirely independent of my dramatic wind ridge.

Good.

I wanted that.

Home not frozen.

Me not frozen either.

I sat on low wall beside steaming drain.

Maro found me after few minutes.

He held two cups.

"Tea."

"Free?"

"Station kitchen."

"Best price."

He sat.

We watched steam.

After while he said, "You look happier."

"Bath."

"I meant trip."

I thought.

"Yes."

"Good."

"That's all?"

"You want speech?"

"No. Last one was upsetting."

"Good."

We drank.

No revelation.

Didn't need one.

I was nineteen.

Again.

Four hundred chapters worth of life would have sounded absurd if chapters existed.

They did not.

Days did.

Road did.

Tomorrow did.

White Span waited six miles north.

Home waited much farther south.

For first time since leaving Carrow, neither direction felt like mistake.

Sojourner.

Temporary resident of everywhere between.
